pos: n. (city of Languedoc; the strongest Huguenot city in France, and the scene of the Michelade of 1567)
etymology: From Latin Nemausus, the Roman colony and its spring deity; French Nimes.
biblical_def: Nimes was the most thoroughly Protestant large city in France: by the 1560s the Reformed held the consulate, the schools and the pulpits, and its academy trained ministers for the whole Midi. It is also the site of one of the Reformation's own atrocities. On the thirtieth of September 1567, the feast of St Michael, a Protestant crowd seized the Catholic clergy and notables of the city and killed about eighty of them, throwing many of the bodies into a well in the bishop's courtyard; the event is called the Michelade. The dictionary records it plainly, because a confessional dictionary that reports only the massacres committed against its own side is not telling the truth. Protestants did this, it was murder, and no provocation excuses it. “For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God” (1Pe 4:17), and the first duty of the house of God in such a case is confession.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a massacre as the slaughter of numbers of human beings with circumstances of cruelty and without authority or necessity, to confess as to own or acknowledge a crime or fault, and sin as any violation of God's commands.
webster_full: MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty; the indiscriminate killing of human beings, without authority or necessity.
CONFESS', v.t. To own, acknowledge or avow, as a crime, a fault, a charge.
SIN, n. 1. The voluntary departure of a moral agent from a known rule of rectitude or duty, prescribed by God; any violation of God’s commands.
ACAD'EMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university or college, and a common school.
scriptures: For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God: and if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
Psa 51:4
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
corruption_summary: The strongest Huguenot city of France, and the Michelade of September 1567, in which a Protestant crowd murdered some eighty Catholics.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is partisan church history: the practice of recounting every wrong suffered by one's own communion and quietly omitting the wrongs it committed. It is a live temptation in Reformed writing about France, where the Huguenots were overwhelmingly the victims and were also, at Nimes, the murderers. A history that cannot say so has made its party the standard instead of the word of God.

The principle to recover is that judgment begins with the household of faith and that the only honest answer to its sin is confession. The order is given: “For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God” (1Pe 4:17). Concealment forfeits mercy and confession secures it: “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13). The offence is against God first, whatever the human provocation: “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight” (Psa 51:4). And the promise to a confessing church is unqualified: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1Jo 1:9).

“Against thee, thee only, have I sinned” (Psa 51:4) — a Protestant city, and a Protestant murder.

pos: n. (fortified Huguenot city of Quercy; held against Louis XIII's siege in 1621, and seat of a Reformed academy)
etymology: From Occitan Montalban, the white hill; French Montauban.
biblical_def: Montauban was one of the places de surete granted to the Huguenots by the Edict of Nantes, and the most stubborn of them. Its academy, moved from Nimes, trained ministers from 1598; its walls were rebuilt and manned by its own citizens; and in the autumn of 1621 it held out for eleven weeks against Louis XIII in person with an army of twenty thousand, until the king broke off the siege with heavy losses. It fell at last in 1629, when the Peace of Alais ended the Huguenot military position for good, and the fortifications came down. The dictionary records Montauban with care, because it is exactly the sort of victory that teaches the wrong lesson. Walls that held once do not hold always, and Scripture puts the matter beyond dispute: “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bulwark as a bastion or rampart capable of resisting cannon shot, to fortify as to surround with works in order to defend against an enemy, and safety as freedom from danger and exemption from hurt.
webster_full: BUL'WARK, n. A bastion, or a rampart; a mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting cannon shot; a fortification.
FORTIFY, v.t. To surround with a wall, ditch, palisades or other works, with a view to defend against the attacks of an enemy.
SAFETY, n. Freedom from danger; exemption from hurt, injury or loss.
HOST, n. An army; a number of men embodied for war; a great multitude.
scriptures: Isa 26:1
In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength.
Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man.
corruption_summary: A Huguenot place of surety whose citizens broke Louis XIII's siege in 1621, and whose walls came down in 1629.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the confidence a church takes in its own defences — a charter, an endowment, a legal protection, a political arrangement — once those defences have held a serious attack. Montauban held in 1621 and was dismantled eight years later by the same king.

The principle to recover is that the only walls that cannot be reduced are the ones God appoints. The prophet puts the fortification in God's hands: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1). Preparation is right and insufficient: “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31). Numbers and strength decide nothing: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an host” (Psa 33:16). And the psalmist asks accordingly: “Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man” (Psa 60:11).

pos: n. (sovereign principality on the Meuse; a Protestant asylum, with an academy from 1579 to 1681)
etymology: From Old French Sedan, of uncertain sense, perhaps from a word for a slope or seat.
biblical_def: Sedan was not in France. It was a sovereign principality held by the La Marck and then the La Tour d'Auvergne dukes of Bouillon, Protestant princes whose independence made the town a legal refuge for Frenchmen who had none; a Reformed academy was founded there in 1579 and taught until 1681, and Pierre Du Moulin, the ablest French Reformed controversialist of his generation, spent his last thirty years in its chair. When Louis XIV absorbed the principality the asylum ended, and four years after the academy closed the Edict of Nantes was revoked. The dictionary records Sedan because the ministry of a refuge is a real ministry, and Scripture speaks of such a place as a man: “a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest” (Isa 32:2). Somebody has to be the covert, and for a century that somebody was a small duchy on the Meuse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covert as a shelter, a defence, a hiding place; an asylum as a place of retreat and security, a refuge; and a shadow as shade within defined limits.
webster_full: COVERT, n. A shelter; a defense; a thicket; a hiding place.
ASY'LUM, n. A place of retreat and security; a refuge; an institution for the protection or relief of the unfortunate.
SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light, apparent on a plane and representing the form of the body which intercepts the rays of light.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.
scriptures: Isa 32:2
And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
Isa 16:4
Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler: for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land.
In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge.
Psa 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
corruption_summary: A sovereign Protestant principality on the Meuse, with Du Moulin in its academy, which sheltered Frenchmen until Louis XIV absorbed it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that giving refuge is charity rather than duty, so that a congregation or a country may decline it without guilt whenever it is inconvenient. Moab was commanded to shelter Israel's outcasts and judged for refusing, and the duchy of Bouillon did for a century what France would not do.

The principle to recover is that God provides coverts for His afflicted people, often through particular men and particular places, and that to be such a covert is an honour. The prophet's image is personal: “a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place” (Isa 32:2). The command to a neighbouring people is explicit: “Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler” (Isa 16:4). The promise runs to the generations: “In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge” (Pro 14:26). And the ultimate covert is God Himself: “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psa 91:1).

pos: n. (city of Languedoc; besieged in 1622, and the place of the peace that ended the Huguenot wars)
etymology: From Occitan Montpeslier, of disputed sense, perhaps the hill of the young maiden or of the spelt.
biblical_def: Montpellier was a Huguenot stronghold and the place where the Huguenot cause was settled on paper. Louis XIII besieged the city through the summer of 1622, could not take it, and signed the Peace of Montpellier in October: the Edict of Nantes was confirmed, liberty of worship was granted, political assemblies were forbidden, and the fortifications of the Protestant towns were to come down except at La Rochelle and Montauban. It was presented as peace and functioned as disarmament; La Rochelle fell in 1628, Alais followed in 1629, and the Revocation came in 1685. The dictionary records Montpellier because the pattern is permanent: a settlement that gives a church words and takes away its standing. “They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 6:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an edict as that which is proclaimed by authority as a rule of action, a revocation as the act of recalling or annulling, as the revocation of an edict, and peace as a state of quiet and freedom from disturbance.
webster_full: EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince.
REVOCA'TION, n. The act of recalling or annulling; repeal; as the revocation of an edict.
PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation.
FORTIFY, v.t. To surround with a wall, ditch, palisades or other works, with a view to defend against the attacks of an enemy.
scriptures: Jer 6:14
They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter:
Mic 3:5
Thus saith the LORD concerning the prophets that make my people err, that bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace; and he that putteth not into their mouths, they even prepare war against him.
There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.
corruption_summary: Besieged by Louis XIII in 1622; the peace signed there confirmed Huguenot worship and dismantled Huguenot defences.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the false peace offered to the church on terms that sound generous: you may believe and worship, provided you give up every means by which you could resist being prevented. The settlement at Montpellier was of exactly that kind, and it was honoured for sixty-three years.

The principle to recover is that a peace announced where there is no peace is named in Scripture as a false prophet's work. The diagnosis is Jeremiah's: “They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 6:14). Ezekiel adds the image of the wall and the bad mortar: “they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace” (Eze 13:10). Micah names the men who cry it and what they do to the man who will not pay them: they “cry, Peace; and he that putteth not into their mouths, they even prepare war against him” (Mic 3:5). And the true state of the matter is declared: “There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked” (Isa 57:21).

pos: n. (town in Champagne; the massacre of March 1562 that began the French wars of religion)
etymology: From Latin Vassiacum, the estate of Vassius; French Vassy, also written Wassy.
biblical_def: Vassy is a small town in Champagne where, on the first of March 1562, the Duke of Guise and his armed retinue came upon a Reformed congregation of several hundred at worship in a barn, and killed somewhere between fifty and eighty of them, wounding many more. The Edict of January, two months old, had expressly permitted such assemblies outside walled towns. The massacre was not punished; it was celebrated at court; and it began eight civil wars that ran for thirty-six years. The dictionary records Vassy because the first act of that long war was the killing of unarmed worshippers by a nobleman who was never called to account in this world. Scripture does not leave such blood unaddressed. “the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” (Gen 4:10) is the standing answer to every unpunished massacre, and the account is kept.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a massacre as the slaughter of numbers with circumstances of cruelty and without authority or necessity, innocent as free from guilt and not having violated any law, and slaughter as destruction of life by violence.
webster_full: MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty; the indiscriminate killing of human beings, without authority or necessity.
INNOCENT, a. Free from guilt; not having done wrong or violated any law.
SLAUGHTER, n. slaw'ter. [Sax. slaht, from slean, to slay.] A killing; destruction of life by violence.
BLOOD, n. [Sax. blod.] The fluid which circulates through the arteries and veins of the human body. Hence, in Scripture, life itself; also, slaughter, murder, the guilt of murder.
scriptures: Gen 4:10
And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.
Pro 6:17
A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood,
Isa 59:7
Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood: their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; wasting and destruction are in their paths.
And in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints, and of all that were slain upon the earth.
corruption_summary: The massacre of a Reformed congregation at worship, first of March 1562, which began thirty-six years of civil war.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the even-handed framing that calls the French wars a conflict between two intolerant parties and leaves it there. Both sides did wrong, and Nimes is in this dictionary to prove that it will say so; but the war began with armed men killing unarmed worshippers who were acting within the law, and that fact is not softened by what came later.

The principle to recover is that shed blood cries to God and is reckoned by Him. The first murder set the pattern: “the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” (Gen 4:10). The shedding of innocent blood stands in the short list of things God hates: “A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood” (Pro 6:17). The prophet describes the eagerness of it: “Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood” (Isa 59:7). And the final account is kept against the persecuting power itself: “in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints” (Rev 18:24).

“hands that shed innocent blood” (Pro 6:17) — a congregation assembled lawfully under the Edict of January.
“in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints” (Rev 18:24) — celebrated at court, and never punished.

pos: n. (city of Languedoc; seat of the chambre de l'edit, the mixed court for Protestant causes)
etymology: From Latin castra, a camp; Occitan and French Castres.
biblical_def: Castres housed one of the most interesting institutions the Edict of Nantes created. The edict of 1598 provided that causes involving Protestants in the southern parlements should be heard not by the ordinary bench but by a chambre de l'edit, a chamber in which Reformed judges sat alongside Catholic ones; the chamber for Toulouse sat at Castres from 1595, with interruptions, until 1679. Its record was mixed and its existence was remarkable: a kingdom that would not grant religious equality nevertheless conceded that a man should not be tried for his property by a bench that regarded his religion as a crime. The dictionary records Castres because impartiality in judgment is a biblical requirement and not a modern invention. “Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great” (Deu 1:17), and the reason given is the weightiest possible: the judgment is God's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an edict as that which is proclaimed by authority as a rule of action, a person as an individual human being consisting of body and soul, and judgment as the sentence pronounced on any person or thing.
webster_full: EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince.
PERSON, n. An individual human being consisting of body and soul.
JUDGMENT, n. The sentence or doom pronounced on any person or thing.
JUS'TICE, n. The virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due; practical conformity to the laws and to principles of rectitude.
scriptures: Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.
Deu 1:17

Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's: and the cause that is too hard for you, bring it unto me, and I will hear it.
These things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment.
Joh 7:24
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
corruption_summary: The chambre de l'edit for the Toulouse parlement, where Reformed judges sat with Catholic ones from 1595 to 1679.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern doctrine that a judge's commitments should shape his verdicts, which is offered as honesty and is simply respect of persons under a new name. Castres was a concession to the opposite principle, made by a government that had every interest in the other.

The principle to recover is that judgment must be rendered without regard to the standing of the parties, and that this is required because the judgment belongs to God. The law forbids partiality in both directions: “thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty” (Lev 19:15). The charge to judges is given with its ground: “ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's” (Deu 1:17). It is repeated among the sayings of the wise: “It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment” (Pro 24:23). And the Lord Himself states the rule: “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment” (Joh 7:24).

pos: n. (town of the Rouergue; seat of the Huguenot political assemblies of 1573 and 1574)
etymology: From Latin Amiliavum, an estate name; Occitan Milhau, French Millau.
biblical_def: Millau was where the Huguenots organised themselves into a state. After the massacre of St Bartholomew in 1572 the southern churches concluded that they could no longer rely on royal protection, and the political assemblies held at Millau in 1573 and 1574 established a federation of the Protestant towns of the Midi with a protector, a council, a treasury, an army and the power to tax — effectively a republic inside the kingdom. It was a defensive measure of a provisional kind, and it was also the thing the crown could never forgive; the ban on political assemblies in every subsequent settlement goes back to Millau. The dictionary records the town because self-government under threat requires men willing to stand up and be counted, and Scripture asks the question directly: “Who will rise up for me against the evildoers?” (Psa 94:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a reproach as censure in terms of opprobrium or contempt, to defend as to uphold or support against attack, and an assembly as a collection of individuals in the same place for the same purpose.
webster_full: REPROACH, v.t. To censure in terms of opprobrium or contempt.
DEFEND', v.t. To maintain or vindicate; to uphold or support against attack; to repel an accusation.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company or collection of individuals, in the same place; usually for the same purpose.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct.
scriptures: Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? or who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity?
Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Neh 4:14

And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.
Pro 31:8
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
corruption_summary: The Huguenot political assemblies of 1573 and 1574, which built a federation of the Midi with a council, a treasury and an army.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the quietism that reads every Christian duty as private, so that organised, lawful, collective self-defence by a persecuted church is treated as a lapse of faith. Scripture knows a different pattern: Nehemiah armed the builders and told them why.

The principle to recover is that God's people may organise, build and defend, and that someone must be willing to be the one who does it. The question is posed as a rebuke to the uninvolved: “Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? or who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity?” (Psa 94:16). Nehemiah's summons names the distress and the remedy together: “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17). The defence is for households and not for glory: “fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses” (Neh 4:14). And speech on behalf of the defenceless is commanded: “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Pro 31:8).

roots_lines: Hebrew qum (H6965) — to rise, to stand up for a cause; Psalm 94:16.
Hebrew raah (H7451) — evil, wickedness, the evildoer's work; Psalm 94:16.

“fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters” (Neh 4:14) — and the ban on political assemblies ever after.

pos: n. (town of the Vivarais; stormed and burned by Louis XIII in May 1629)
etymology: From Occitan Privas, of uncertain sense, perhaps from a Latin personal name.
biblical_def: Privas was the chief Protestant town of the Vivarais and was destroyed for it. In May 1629, in the last campaign of the Huguenot wars, Louis XIII took the town by storm; the garrison and a large part of the population were killed, the houses were burned, and the king forbade the place to be rebuilt, though the ban was later relaxed. The Peace of Alais followed within weeks and ended the Huguenot military and political existence altogether, leaving only the liberty of worship that would itself be revoked in 1685. The dictionary records Privas because Scripture gives the church words for this and expects it to use them. Lament is a biblical act, and the ruin of a town is a proper subject for it: “Your country is desolate, your cities are burned with fire” (Isa 1:7). So is the resolve that follows lament in Habakkuk, who lists every loss and then rejoices anyway.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines desolate as destitute of inhabitants, laid waste, in a ruinous condition; to spoil as to plunder or strip by violence; and a sanctuary as a sacred place.
webster_full: DESOLATE, a. Destitute of inhabitants; deserted; uninhabited; laid waste; in a ruinous condition.
SPOIL, v.t. To plunder; to strip by violence; to take by force from an enemy.
SANCTUARY, n. [L. sanctuarium, from sanctus, sacred.] A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple, called the Holy of Holies.
FIRE, n. The effect of combustion. The combustion of inflammable substances, producing heat and light.
scriptures: Isa 1:7
Your country is desolate, your cities are burned with fire: your land, strangers devour it in your presence, and it is desolate, as overthrown by strangers.
Jer 4:20
Destruction upon destruction is cried; for the whole land is spoiled: suddenly are my tents spoiled, and my curtains in a moment.
Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
Hab 3:17

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
corruption_summary: The chief Protestant town of the Vivarais, stormed and burned in May 1629, weeks before the Peace of Alais.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern impatience with lament, which hurries a suffering church past its grief to a lesson or a resolution. Scripture devotes whole books to the words a ruined people should say, and it does not hurry them.

The principle to recover is that the church is given a vocabulary for devastation and is meant to speak it before God. The prophet describes without softening: “Your country is desolate, your cities are burned with fire” (Isa 1:7). The suddenness is part of the complaint: “Destruction upon destruction is cried; for the whole land is spoiled” (Jer 4:20). Even the burning of the place of worship is brought to God rather than explained away: “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7). And when every earthly support is gone the prophet still turns, after the full inventory of loss: “Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines” (Hab 3:17).

pos: n. (city of Normandy; a Reformed academy and the chair of Samuel Bochart the orientalist)
etymology: From Gaulish Catumagus, the field of battle; Norman French Caen.
biblical_def: Caen was the chief Protestant centre of Normandy and the seat of a Reformed academy whose particular strength was the oriental languages. Samuel Bochart served the church there from 1626 until his death in 1667, and wrote two works that were consulted for two centuries: a geography of the nations of Genesis and a study of the animals of Scripture, both built on Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic sources which he read himself. He was invited to Sweden by Queen Christina and went back to Caen. The dictionary records the city because this kind of labour — years spent on the grammar of a language in order to settle the sense of a verse — is the unglamorous foundation of every faithful translation and commentary. “If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4) is the condition; the tongues are part of the digging.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to search as to look over or through for the purpose of finding something, treasure as wealth accumulated or a store in reserve, and the tongue as the instrument of speech and the power of articulate utterance.
webster_full: SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through for the purpose of finding something; to examine; to explore.
TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; the power of articulate utterance.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
scriptures: Pro 2:4
If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures;
Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O LORD God of hosts.
More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.
corruption_summary: Normandy's Reformed academy, and Bochart's forty years on the geography and the animals of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the popular preference for a devotional reading that needs no labour, and the matching assumption that a man who spends decades on Syriac has lost the plot. Every English Bible the reader trusts rests on men who did exactly that.

The principle to recover is that the meaning of Scripture is to be dug for, and that the digging is honourable work. The condition attached to finding is effort: “If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4). What God has hidden, men in authority are honoured for tracing out: “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter” (Pro 25:2). The end of it is not information but nourishment: “Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart” (Jer 15:16). And the result is a valuation: “More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold” (Psa 19:10).

“Thy words were found, and I did eat them” (Jer 15:16) — invited to Sweden, and returned to Normandy.

pos: n. (Norman seaport; an early Reformed church, and the harbour of the Huguenot dispersion)
etymology: From Old Norse djupr, deep, of the deep harbour; French Dieppe.
biblical_def: Dieppe was one of the first French towns to have a Reformed church, organised in the 1550s among its seamen and merchants, and it was one of the last doors out. Its ships carried Huguenots to England, to the Netherlands and across the Atlantic; the French settlements in Canada were largely manned from Dieppe, and after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 a steady traffic of refugees left its quays, lawfully or otherwise, for Rye and Dover. The dictionary records Dieppe because the dispersion of the French Protestants was one of the great migrations of church history, and it went by sea, in small boats, family by family. “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23) names the men who did it, and the promise for the crossing is given to such people: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee” (Isa 43:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the sea as a large body of salt water, a ship as a vessel adapted to navigation, and a refuge as shelter or protection from danger or distress.
webster_full: SEA, n. [Sax. sae.] A large body of salt water, less than an ocean; also, the ocean in general.
SHIP, n. In a general sense, a vessel or building of a peculiar structure, adapted to navigation.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.
EXILE, n. The state of being banished from one's country; the person banished.
scriptures: They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;
Isa 43:2

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea;
Behold, these shall come from far: and, lo, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim.
corruption_summary: An early Reformed church among Norman seamen, and the harbour from which the Huguenot dispersion sailed after 1685.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the sentimental picture of migration, which makes the refugee either a hero or a statistic. The people who left Dieppe were ordinary tradesmen with children, breaking the law of their country to attend public worship, and paying a boatman to take them across at night.

The principle to recover is that God's hand is not shortened by distance or by water. The psalmist marks out the seafarers as a class who see His works: “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23). The promise for the passage is express: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee” (Isa 43:2). No distance removes a man from Him: “If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea” (Psa 139:9). And the gathering of the scattered is foretold from every quarter: “these shall come from far: and, lo, these from the north and from the west” (Isa 49:12).

“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee” (Isa 43:2) — refugees for Rye and Dover after 1685.
“these shall come from far” (Isa 49:12) — the Huguenot dispersion, family by family.
